claims.text: An adaptive machine-learning-enhanced free-energy protocol can accurately reproduce fusion thermodynamic properties in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The proposed protocol will reduce computational cost by at least an order of magnitude relative to TOR-TILD.
The proposed protocol will reduce computational cost by at least an order of magnitude relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The target material is an equimolar multicomponent high-entropy alloy such as CoCrFeMnNi near its fusion point.
The ML potential will be trained on targeted ab initio snapshots from both solid and liquid states near the fusion temperature.
The workflow will combine active-learning thermodynamic integration with small-scale ab initio MD corrections directed at electron–vibration coupling.
The protocol is intended to operate within 100 K above or below the expected melting point.
The ML potential can serve as a surrogate for the ab initio potential-energy surface in phase free-energy calculations.
Thermodynamic integration and enhanced sampling using the surrogate potential can mediate the calculated free-energy difference between solid and liquid phases.
Active learning will identify configuration-space regions in which the initial ML potential deviates from the ab initio description.
Selective ab initio MD corrections will refine the ML potential in the regions identified by active learning.
The iterative refinement will preserve anharmonic vibrational and electron–vibration contributions across the phase transition.
Fusion free-energy differences, latent heat, and vibrational entropy differences will agree with full ab initio MD to within approximately 5%.
The computational cost will be at least tenfold lower than TOR-TILD and will be reduced by an even larger factor relative to direct ab initio MD.
Existing explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD results for elemental and binary systems can provide accuracy and cost baselines.
Elemental Al and binary Cu–Zr systems are suitable initial validation systems before extension to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Deviation of more than approximately 5% from explicit ab initio MD in phase free-energy differences or derived observables would falsify the claimed fidelity.
